projects.name: Mo3ta
projects.summary: Palestine's statistics in one place: dashboards, a map and charts over a large Arabic dataset, rendered on the server so every number can be found and cited.

case.lede: Palestine's statistics in one place: dashboards, a map and charts over a large Arabic dataset. A journalist, a researcher or a student should be able to find a number, see it in context and cite it.
glance: UX and UI design, then the whole build
Numbers in Arabic, map and chart components, server rendering
Vue 3 and Inertia with SSR, on Laravel
case.decision: Keep everything around the data quiet so the map and the charts carry the colour, and never show a number without its date and its source.

evidence.alt: Mo3ta's daily dashboard in Arabic: six headline counts, a search field, region and period filters, and the top of a map.
evidence.caption: The daily dashboard. Region, period and governorate filters sit above the map, and the date of the last update is in the header.

evidence.alt: Mo3ta's home page on a phone: a map of Palestine with four headline counts placed around it.
evidence.caption: The home page at phone width. The map stays in the middle of the screen.

evidence.alt: The daily dashboard on a phone: counts in two columns, then search, region chips, a governorate menu and period tabs.
evidence.caption: The same dashboard on a phone. The counts drop to two columns and the filters stack under the search.

story.p: Before this, the statistics lived in PDFs and spreadsheets. The centre wanted one place where a number could be found, seen on a map or a chart, and cited.

story.h: Why every page renders on the server
story.p: A figure that search engines cannot read is a figure nobody finds, so a client-only dashboard was ruled out early. Pages are rendered on the server with Inertia and arrive as real HTML, and Vue 3 adds the interactive layer on top.

story.h: One component set for every figure
story.p: The map and the charts are one reusable set, fed from the same indicator model, with export and share on each figure. They use the same tokens as the marketing pages, so the product and the site look like one thing.
Figures sit on a monospaced scale so they line up in columns. The layout runs right to left throughout, and the axes and legends are placed so they still read naturally that way.

result: Live at mo3ta.ps, with the indicator library, the map and the dashboards in production.
todo: Mo3ta's result is only 'live'. If the centre can share anything public (usage, citations, press), add it to case.result.
An early sketch or a rejected version of the dashboard would show the decisions better than the final screen alone.

projects.name: Devlo CMS
projects.role: Design, front-end and back-end; product owner of the front-end
projects.summary: One Laravel application running 24 Arabic news sites, each with its own theme, modules, languages and editorial team.

case.lede: One Laravel application runs 24 Arabic news sites, each with its own theme, modules, languages and editorial team. I designed the editorial panel and the theming model, then built both.
glance: Design and full-stack, product owner of the front-end
Theming model, a panel in three languages, guard rails
Blade, Livewire and Alpine on Laravel; MySQL, Redis
case.decision: A site may differ in configuration, not in behaviour. Every newsroom runs the same modules and the same code; what changes is the theme, the languages and which modules are switched on.

evidence.caption: Six of the 24 sites. Same codebase and same modules; the themes, the languages and the switched-on modules differ.

evidence.alt: Quds News Network's front page on a phone: the lead story over a photo, then a list of headlines with thumbnails.
evidence.caption: Quds News Network at phone width. Its front page is assembled from the same modules as the others.

story.p: Newsrooms used to be built one at a time, each a fork of the last. A fix in one site never reached the others, and every new client meant weeks of repeated work. Share previews show what that costs after a few years: each theme had grown its own share handler, and some fell back to a favicon, which WhatsApp will not turn into a card.

Front pages are built from shared modules: a breaking strip, a lead story, a headline rail, an audio briefing, podcast and translation sections. Editors switch them on per site. A new feature starts switched off everywhere and is turned on for one site in the same commit that writes it, so the question of who gets it is answered before it ships.

story.h: A theme from a brand book
story.p: IWAD is one of the themes: a research platform for a defence institute, 24 pages, right to left. The brand book was six pages and had no type scale, spacing or components, so those were designed first, in two written documents, and the pages were built on them. Sections are told apart by colour instead of icons, because anything military reads as combat. It is live at wardefense.institute.

story.h: A panel that shows only what a newsroom uses
story.p: The editorial panel works in Arabic, English and Turkish, right to left by default. Switching a module off removes its route, its sidebar entry and its permission together, so an editor never meets a menu item that leads nowhere. Every label is a translation key, 5,874 of them, checked in CI.

Share previews run through one controller for every site. The site name is not added to the title, because WhatsApp and Telegram give the title a single line and the prefix was eating the part of the headline that earns the click. Descriptions stop at 200 characters, which still reads as a full sentence on every platform.

story.h: Checks for what nobody can see
story.p: Some failures never throw an error: an English string that renders in Arabic because Arabic is the fallback, a share image a crawler quietly refuses, a permission that exists on one route and nowhere else. Each has a command that fails before a commit lands, across 456 Livewire components and 839 Blade views.

Maktoob Media, the English site on the platform, felt slow on mobile. Lighthouse against production moved 20 points between identical runs, so before touching the site I built a rig that could tell two builds apart. Fonts went from 749 KB to 78 KB and icons from 302 KB to 31.6 KB. The usual advice, content-visibility on the off-screen sections, measured 84 against 83 and was thrown away.

result: Runs 24 sites, among them Quds News Network, Maktoob Media, Tayaqan, Hodhod, Adeni Cast and the Saleh Al-Arouri archive.
Quds News Network, real Chrome users over 28 days: FAST, with LCP at 2.33 s and INP at 104 ms.
case.reflection: The guard commands arrived after the failures they catch, one at a time, each written the day something silent reached a client. They should have come first for each part of the system. Writing the check first forces you to decide what correct means, and that was the part that was actually missing.
todo: Devlo's evidence is the sites, not the panel: demo.taktek.co/dashboard redirects to a login, so the editorial panel could not be captured. A screenshot of the panel (dashboard, sidebar, a module switched off) would show the design side directly.

The old Quds case credited Quds with the 749 KB to 78 KB font cut. Your GitHub write-up places that audit on maktoobmedia.com, so it now sits under Maktoob. If Quds got the same pass, add it back to the Quds paragraph.

IWAD is live at wardefense.institute, but its sections are still empty, so the grid shows the theme build with sample content. Recapture the hubs from the live site once the first publications are out.

projects.name: Kevla Campa
projects.summary: A design concept for a Kevlar and carbon-fibre caravan maker: scroll scenes on CSS view timelines, no build step, no axe-core violations across 24 page states. Placeholder copy, not a client launch.

case.lede: A marketing site for KEVLA CAMPA, a teardrop caravan built as one Kevlar and carbon-fibre shell. It is a design concept, not a launched site: I designed it and wrote all of it by hand, in HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework and no build step.
glance: Scroll scenes that explain the shell, motion that stays smooth, accessibility checked
HTML, CSS and ES modules; no framework, no build step

evidence.alt: The Kevla Campa home page: the headline Built different. over a photo of the white caravan, with Explore Kevla and Enquire now buttons.
evidence.caption: The home page, the first of four pinned scenes. As the page scrolls, the photo drifts and scales under the headline.

evidence.alt: The home page on a phone: the headline, both buttons and the four selling points in two columns.
evidence.caption: The home page at phone width. The four selling points drop into two columns.

evidence.alt: The caravan explorer on a phone: view tabs, the caravan photo with numbered hotspots, and the notes for hotspot 08, the monocoque shell.
evidence.caption: The explorer on a phone. The hotspots stay on the photo, and the notes for the selected one sit under it.

case.decision: The scroll does the explaining. The home page walks through the shell in four pinned scenes, from the laminate to the places it goes, and each scene is a CSS animation on its own view timeline, not a script listening to the scroll.

system.title: The system: a dark shell, one lime accent

swatches.name: Surface
swatches.role: Photo frames, tiles and the explorer

swatches.name: Light
swatches.role: The light sections, set in ink

swatches.name: Lime
swatches.role: Links, focus and selection, 10.2:1 on the ground

swatches.name: Cyan
swatches.role: Hover and section labels on the dark

swatches.name: Cyan on light
swatches.role: The same job on light sections, 5.9:1

system.note: Archivo carries everything large, widened to between 110 and 118 percent, and Azeret Mono carries the labels, never below 11 px. The cyan falls to 2.1:1 on the light sections, so they get a darker one, and every translucent colour is mixed from these tokens with color-mix().

grid.caption: Four of the seven pages: the home page halfway through the laminate scan, the construction page, the caravan explorer and the gallery filters.

items.label: Home, mid-scroll
items.alt: The laminate scan part way through: a green line has uncovered the finished white caravan over a raw carbon weave.

items.label: The Kevla
items.alt: The technology page: the headline The skin is the structure, over a close-up of the shell.

items.label: The Caravan
items.alt: The caravan explorer: the caravan photo with eight numbered hotspots beside the notes for the selected one.

items.label: Gallery
items.alt: The gallery: filter chips for all, exterior, detail and environment above a grid of photos.

story.p: The home page pins four scenes: the hero, a scan that turns raw laminate into the finished shell, a track through the places it goes, and a closing call to action. Each one is a keyframe animation on the view timeline of its section, so it runs off the main thread. Browsers without scroll timelines get a small script that seeks the same keyframes, and with reduced motion or JavaScript off the page is a plain, fully visible layout.

The adventure track felt jerky. Rendering held 60 fps, with a 95th-percentile frame of 16.8 ms even at four times CPU throttling, so the fault was the motion itself: each move was squeezed into 12% of the scene and jumped up to 296 px in a frame. The track now rests on each panel and glides over 16% on a sine curve, which cut the jump to 73 px at 1440 px wide and 16 px on a phone, and no headline is ever shown clipped.

The menu, the enquiry drawer and the gallery lightbox are native dialogs, so focus trapping and Escape come from the browser. They animate out as well as in, and pages crossfade in 220 ms with cross-document view transitions while the header holds still.

On the caravan page the hotspots stay locked to the photo at every size, and each one fills the detail panel with its own photo and notes. The next photo swaps in only once it has decoded, so the panel never flashes empty.

The figures from the maker were not supplied, so none were invented: the specification sheet reads Awaiting client figures, the story copy is marked DUMMY, and the phone number sits in a range reserved for fiction. The README lists everything to replace before launch.

story.h: Fonts that do not move the page
story.p: Archivo and Azeret Mono are self-hosted variable fonts with fallbacks sized from the font files, so the text takes nearly the same space before and after the fonts arrive, and layout shift stays at 0 on every page.

result: A design concept: not launched, and every stand-in on it is marked as one.

No axe-core violations across 24 states, every page at desktop and phone widths plus the open dialogs and form errors, and 100 for accessibility, best practices and SEO in Lighthouse on every page, from the runs recorded in the repository.
The code, the README and the six motion plans behind the changes are public.
case.reflection: Put the buttons in the hero on screen sooner. They finish arriving at about 2.35 seconds; the motion audit in the repository noted it and left it for later, and a shorter, regular stagger would fix it.
todo: Kevla Campa is shown as a design concept. If the maker saw it or it led to work, add that here; until then the case says concept.

projects.name: FreightZone
projects.client: Freight marketplace, client and driver apps
projects.role: Product design: UX, UI and the design system
projects.summary: A two-sided freight marketplace for Australia, designed end to end: clients post a job, drivers bid, and payment is held in escrow until delivery is confirmed. A client app and a driver app, 70+ screens and states on one design system.
projects.alt: FreightZone app design: delivery tracking, a three-bid comparison and the escrow payment screen
projects.caption: Figma case study, 70+ screens and states

case.lede: A local freight marketplace for Australia. Clients post a delivery request, drivers bid, the client picks an offer and pays into escrow, and the driver is paid once delivery is confirmed. I took an existing set of screens and turned it into a complete, testable two-sided product on one design system.
glance: Product designer: UX, UI and the design system
iOS and Android, on a 360 x 800 base
Client app and driver app, 70+ screens and states

evidence.alt: The FreightZone cover: the headline From pickup to final delivery beside three phone screens, a delivery in transit, three bids to compare and a payment secured in escrow.
evidence.caption: The cover of the design file: tracking, the bid comparison and the escrow confirmation, three of the 70+ screens and states.

case.decision: Every bid looks the same. Clients choose between people and prices, so each bid card carries the same five facts in the same place: price, pickup time, delivery estimate, vehicle and rating. A compare view lines up to three bids in one table and marks the best value in each row.

system.title: The system: the client's red, made to pass
system.note: The logo and the red were kept, but the red went from #F81D3E to #D7102F so white text passes WCAG AA. Plus Jakarta Sans runs in 11 styles from Display 32 down to 12 px and never smaller; radius tokens are bound to variables, spacing sits on a 4-point grid with a 20 px screen margin, and icon buttons are at least 44 x 44.

story.p: “Get a quote” went straight to payment without ever showing a price, a vehicle or a pickup time. Phone login, an email password reset and Google sign-in sat side by side with no password field anywhere. The same code meant two different things on two screens, a nine-item drawer hid the core tasks, and only the happy path existed.

Senders who want the price and the pickup time before they pay, and independent drivers who want to be verified quickly and to see fare and distance before they accept. Both are proto-personas: there was no research budget, and the file labels them as assumptions.

Post, receive bids, compare, select, pay into escrow, track, confirm, get paid. The drawer became four tabs per app, and both apps share one status badge, from Open for bids to Paid out, so the client and the driver always see the same state name for the same job.

story.h: Trust at the moment of doubt
story.p: Paying a stranger up front is the biggest barrier in the flow, so escrow is explained three times, briefly: when a request is published (nothing is charged now), before a driver is chosen (what happens next) and on the payment screen. Phone OTP is the only sign-in, and only the driver ever types the handover code.

story.h: The states, not just the happy path
story.p: Loading while a driver is matched, empty lists, a wrong code with attempts left, a declined payment with no charge, offline with the last update time, buttons disabled until a code is complete, and success. Motion appears only where it explains something: the onboarding carousel, sheet transitions and a pulse while a driver is found.

result: A complete Figma file for both apps, 70+ screens and states on one design system, with the case study in the same file.

Four hypotheses, each with the metric that would confirm or kill it after launch, from the time it takes to pick a bid to the drop-off between choosing a driver and securing the payment. They are proposals, not results.
